content:
Quick answer: Assistive devices may make a difficult task easier, but the right choice depends on your joints, grip, balance and home. An occupational therapist can assess everyday activities; a physiotherapist can advise on walking aids. Ask about assessed equipment before buying. Availability, eligibility and charges vary across the UK.

Start with the task you want to do, rather than a product labelled "for arthritis". Opening a jar, getting dressed and getting out of a bath involve different movements and risks. Sometimes a different way of doing the task is more useful than another gadget. This guide describes categories to discuss, not tested products or a promise that an aid will treat arthritis.

What NICE recommends

NICE NG226, recommendation 1.3.10, says to consider walking aids, such as sticks, for people with lower-limb osteoarthritis. That is not a recommendation for every person with arthritis to buy a stick. NICE describes walking aids as helping walking pattern, balance or weight bearing; it does not give a universal percentage reduction in joint load for this guide.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE NG100, recommendation 1.8.2, says adults should have access to specialist occupational therapy, with periodic review, if everyday activities or hand function are difficult. Equipment is one possible part of that support. It does not replace your arthritis treatment.

Do not assume every support advertised online is recommended by NICE. NG226 says not to routinely offer insoles, braces, tape, splints or supports for osteoarthritis unless there is joint instability or abnormal loading, exercise is ineffective or unsuitable without the device, and the device is likely to improve movement and function. Discuss your own need with your treating team rather than applying that rule to a different diagnosis.

Kitchen aids: match the tool to the difficulty

  • Electric can openers and jar grippers: options if gripping or twisting is difficult. Designs work differently, so try the action you actually need rather than assuming the tool removes all hand effort.
  • Kettle tippers or kettle holders: support pouring when lifting is difficult. Ask about a model suitable for your kettle and how to use it safely. Do not assume any cradle fits any kettle.
  • Adapted cutlery and two-handled cups: larger or shaped handles may be easier to hold. The most comfortable shape is individual.
  • Food-preparation boards and non-slip mats: can help hold food or crockery steady. Ask for a demonstration, particularly if using a board with spikes or cutting one-handed.

NHS inform's occupational-therapy guide describes these kinds of equipment. The CNTW NHS small-aids leaflet illustrates food-preparation and grip aids and suggests asking an occupational therapist about trying an item. Its examples are not evidence that a named brand is best for arthritis.

Bathroom and toilet equipment

Options to discuss include grab rails, a shower seat, a bath lift, a raised toilet seat or easier-to-turn taps. The NHS home-adaptations guide explains how an assessment can identify changes that suit the person and their home.

For equipment you will lean on, sit on or use to transfer, ask the assessor or supplier to confirm the fit, installation and instructions before use. Check the actual product's weight limit and maintenance information. A list of aids cannot establish that a rail, seat or stool is safe in your bathroom. If getting in or out already feels unsafe, ask for assessment rather than buying by price alone.

Dressing aids

A sock aid, button hook or zip puller can reduce difficult reaching or fiddly fastening. NHS information includes these categories. Ask an occupational therapist which action is causing the problem and whether an aid or a change to clothing would help. Try the item with your own clothes where possible. A gadget should not be assumed suitable simply because another person with arthritis uses it.

Walking sticks, frames and wheelchairs

The NHS walking-aids guide explains that a stick can provide support and balance and may make walking less painful. Ask for the correct height, handle and instructions, including advice about steps. This page does not promise a particular percentage reduction in hip or knee load.

A walking frame is not always a four-wheeled rollator with a seat. Frames come in different designs, including ones without wheels. The NHS advises considering where it will be used, whether you can lift it, its height and whether you need features such as a seat or folding frame. Discuss the choice with a physiotherapist or the team providing the aid.

An NHS wheelchair requires an assessment by the local wheelchair service to decide whether one is needed and which type is suitable. Ask a GP, physiotherapist, occupational therapist or hospital team about referral. Some services accept self-referrals. Provision and any contribution depend on your circumstances; a wheelchair is not automatically supplied because walking longer distances is difficult.

Assessment and help with equipment costs

Ask your GP or treating team about occupational therapy for everyday tasks and physiotherapy for walking-aid advice. For home equipment, contact the appropriate local service directly and ask about its assessment route, eligibility, waiting time and charges before buying.

  • England: the NHS social-care guides explain that council needs and home assessments are free. Equipment and small adaptations may be supplied following assessment. The NHS says councils should pay for adaptations costing less than £1,000. This is not a promise to reimburse an item you buy independently.
  • Scotland: NHS inform says assessed equipment is usually supplied free on long-term loan, but some local authorities charge for some items. Ask your local authority or occupational-therapy service what applies.
  • Northern Ireland: contact your Health and Social Care Trust. nidirect's equipment guide explains the assessment and buying options; some everyday items may need to be paid for privately.
  • Wales: ask your council's social-services team or local health team about the local equipment and occupational-therapy route. For adaptations, GOV.WALES says homeowners should contact the local authority and tenants should contact their landlord. Do not assume the England funding description applies throughout the UK.

NHS sticks and frames may be available to borrow, sometimes with a deposit. Wheelchair services have their own assessment arrangements. A free assessment does not mean every product, adaptation or privately chosen upgrade is free.

Major home adaptations and grants

A stairlift, accessible shower or other major adaptation needs a separate discussion about suitability and funding. GOV.UK's Disabled Facilities Grant page lists maximum grants of £30,000 in England, £36,000 in Wales and £25,000 in Northern Ireland. Scotland has a different equipment-and-adaptations system, not this grant. Some councils may offer more.

These are maximum amounts, not guaranteed awards. Income, savings, age and other eligibility rules affect help and contributions. Contact the relevant council or housing service before starting work: GOV.UK warns that starting before approval may mean no grant. In Northern Ireland, nidirect explains the roles of occupational therapy, your landlord and the Housing Executive.

Hiring or buying without a service promise

The British Red Cross wheelchair-hire page describes a generally paid service, with NHS-funded arrangements for Hampshire, Northern Ireland and Norfolk and Waveney. Check your postcode, eligibility, availability, hire and delivery charges, and return arrangements directly. Do not assume a short-term charity loan is free everywhere.

If buying privately, ask about a demonstration or home trial, fit, returns, delivery, installation, repairs and the total price. The NHS household-equipment guide describes assessment and hire options. This article does not quote current product prices, rank retailers or promise next-day delivery. Check the seller's current terms rather than treating a shop name as an endorsement.

When equipment is not the next step

Do not wait for an aid to arrive if a joint is hot and swollen, or joint pain comes with feeling unwell, fever or shivering. NHS joint-pain advice is to seek an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 help. Use NHS 111 in England, Scotland or Wales; in Northern Ireland contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service when closed.

Go to A&E or call 999 for very bad joint pain after a fall or injury, inability to walk or put weight on a joint, a joint out of place, or tingling or loss of feeling around it after injury. Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency. Equipment is not a substitute for assessing a new injury or infection.

Prepare for an equipment assessment

Write down the task you find difficult, where it happens, what you have tried and how it varies on better and worse days. Bring details of existing aids. The symptom and flare tracker can help organise notes, but it is not a diagnostic tool. Ask who will fit the item, show you how to use it, review it and handle repairs or returns.

Evidence and review scope

NICE recommendations here concern lower-limb osteoarthritis walking aids and specialist occupational therapy in rheumatoid arthritis. They do not endorse every household gadget, product or retailer. NHS and government sources support the practical equipment and access information. Local eligibility and prices can change.
